posts.post_title: Which organism causes anthrax in livestock a…
posts.post_content: Which organism causes anthrax in livestock and human beings?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bacillus anthracis

Bacillus anthracis, a Gram-positive, spore-forming, capsulated bacillus, causes anthrax.

Correct Option Explanation

It is a non-motile, aerobic organism appearing as square-ended rods in short chains, producing resistant environmental spores.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bacillus cereus is a distinct food-poisoning organism, not the anthrax agent.
  • Clostridium chauvoei causes Black Quarter, a different clostridial disease of cattle.
  • Bacillus subtilis is a common non-pathogenic soil saprophyte.
Know More
  • Anthrax is also called Spleenic fever or Milzbrand.
  • Capsule made of poly D-glutamic acid resists phagocytosis.
  • Triple toxin: edema factor, lethal factor, protective antigen.
  • OIE lists it as a Category A bioterrorism agent.

posts.post_title: Which of the following is NOT a recognized s…
posts.post_content: Which of the following is NOT a recognized synonym of anthrax?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Blackleg

Blackleg is not an anthrax synonym; it refers to Black Quarter caused by Cl. chauvoei.

Correct Option Explanation

Anthrax's recognized synonyms are Spleenic fever, Milzbrand, Charbon, Wool sorters disease and Malignant carbuncle.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Milzbrand is a genuine German-origin synonym of anthrax.
  • Charbon is the French-origin synonym for anthrax.
  • Wool sorters disease reflects human infection via inhalation while processing wool.
Know More
  • Anthrax also called Malignant carbuncle.
  • Spleen enlargement gave the name Spleenic fever.
  • Restricted endemic zones are called anthrax belts.
  • Disease is enzootic in India.

posts.post_title: The triple toxin genes of Bacillus anthracis…
posts.post_content: The triple toxin genes of Bacillus anthracis (edema factor, lethal factor, protective antigen) are carried on which plasmid?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: pXO1

The pXO1 plasmid encodes the anthrax triple toxin complex.

Correct Option Explanation

pXO1 codes edema factor-I, lethal factor-II and protective antigen-III, the virulence toxins.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • pXO2 instead encodes the anti-phagocytic poly D-glutamic acid capsule.
  • pBR322 is a laboratory cloning vector unrelated to B. anthracis virulence.
  • F plasmid mediates bacterial conjugation in E. coli, unrelated here.
Know More
  • Vaccine strain Sterne 34F2 is pXO1+/pXO2-.
  • Capsule resists host phagocytosis.
  • At least 3x10^6 bacteria/ml blood needed to cause death.
  • Death mechanism called the 'Log Jam' theory.

posts.post_title: The anti-phagocytic capsule of Bacillus anth…
posts.post_content: The anti-phagocytic capsule of Bacillus anthracis is chemically composed of which substance?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Poly D-glutamic acid

The B. anthracis capsule is made of poly D-glutamic acid, coded by plasmid pXO2.

Correct Option Explanation

This capsule resists phagocytosis by host immune cells, allowing bacterial survival and septicaemia.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Hyaluronic acid forms the capsule of Streptococcus equi (strangles), not B. anthracis.
  • Peptidoglycan is the bacterial cell wall component, not the capsule material.
  • Polysaccharide capsules occur in organisms like Klebsiella, not B. anthracis.
Know More
  • Capsule gene resides on plasmid pXO2.
  • CO2 tension of 5% increases capsule production in culture.
  • Capsulated colonies appear mucoid.
  • Stained pink by McFadyean's reaction.

posts.post_title: McFadyean's reaction, used to diagnose anthr…
posts.post_content: McFadyean's reaction, used to diagnose anthrax on a blood smear, employs which stain?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Polychrome methylene blue

McFadyean's reaction uses ripened polychrome methylene blue stain on a blood smear.

Correct Option Explanation

It reveals square-ended blue bacilli with a metachromatic pink capsule, confirming B. anthracis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Giemsa stain is used for blood parasites like Anaplasma, not this reaction.
  • Gram stain shows B. anthracis as Gram-positive but is not McFadyean's reaction.
  • Ziehl-Neelsen stain detects acid-fast organisms such as Mycobacterium.
Know More
  • Diagnosis avoids blood chemistry work due to human exposure risk.
  • Ascoli's test detects antigen in decayed carcasses.
  • Guinea pig inoculation aids early-stage diagnosis.
  • Real-time PCR is highly sensitive for soil isolates.

posts.post_title: On gelatin stab culture, Bacillus anthracis…
posts.post_content: On gelatin stab culture, Bacillus anthracis growth typically shows which characteristic appearance?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Inverted fir tree appearance

B. anthracis on gelatin stab culture shows an inverted fir tree appearance with slow liquefaction.

Correct Option Explanation

Liquefaction of the gelatin begins from the top, producing this characteristic branching pattern.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Medusa head colonies instead describe its growth on 5% blood agar medium.
  • Fried egg colonies are typical of Mycoplasma, an unrelated organism.
  • Cauliflower growth is not a recognized B. anthracis culture pattern.
Know More
  • Blood agar shows medusa head colonies.
  • Spores are ellipsoidal, central in the sporangium.
  • Spores are highly refractile and resistant to staining.
  • Vaccine strain is non-capsulated and avirulent.

posts.post_title: Which live spore vaccine strain of Bacillus…
posts.post_content: Which live spore vaccine strain of Bacillus anthracis is used for anthrax vaccination in India?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Sterne 34F2

India uses the Sterne 34F2 strain, a non-capsulated, avirulent glycerinated spore vaccine.

Correct Option Explanation

This strain is pXO1-positive/pXO2-negative, so it lacks the capsule but retains protective immunogenicity.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • BCG strain is a tuberculosis vaccine strain, unrelated to anthrax.
  • Brucella S19 is used against bovine brucellosis, not anthrax.
  • 19-strain is not a recognized designation for any anthrax vaccine.
Know More
  • Vaccine also uses Montanide adjuvant for ruminants.
  • Glycerol-suspended vaccine can irritate goats.
  • Immunity develops in about 10 days.
  • Protection lasts 10 months to one year.

posts.post_title: At necropsy, the spleen in an anthrax-affect…
posts.post_content: At necropsy, the spleen in an anthrax-affected animal characteristically shows which appearance?

_aimcq_options.text: Soft, enlarged spleen with blackberry jam consistency

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Soft, enlarged spleen with blackberry jam consistency

Anthrax produces a soft, enlarged spleen with a characteristic blackberry jam consistency.

Correct Option Explanation

This splenic change, along with unclotted tarry blood from natural orifices, is a key necropsy indicator.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • A hard, fibrotic spleen suggests chronic conditions, not acute anthrax.
  • A pale, calcified spleen is not a described anthrax necropsy finding.
  • A normal-sized spleen is inconsistent with the marked enlargement seen in anthrax.
Know More
  • Carcass shows absence of rigor mortis.
  • Posture described as 'saw horse posture'.
  • Pharyngeal lesions in horses/pigs called pharyngeal form.
  • Suspect carcasses must never be opened before diagnosis.

posts.post_title: As per the 'Log Jam' theory, what minimum ba…
posts.post_content: As per the 'Log Jam' theory, what minimum bacterial concentration in blood is necessary to cause death in anthrax?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 3x10^6 bacteria/ml

At least 3x10^6 bacteria/ml of blood is required to cause death in anthrax.

Correct Option Explanation

Capillary blockage by this bacterial load underlies the 'Log Jam' theory of terminal anoxia and shock.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 3x10^3/ml is far below the threshold documented for lethal septicaemia.
  • 3x10^9/ml overstates the documented minimum lethal concentration.
  • 3x10^4/ml is also below the recorded lethal bacterial threshold.
Know More
  • Death results from shock, renal failure and anoxia.
  • Lethal toxin causes edema and tissue damage.
  • In pigs, bacilli localize in throat lymph nodes.
  • Course of acute disease is about 48 hours.

posts.post_title: Which group of animals is described as highl…
posts.post_content: Which group of animals is described as highly susceptible to anthrax compared with goats and horses?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Cattle and sheep

Cattle and sheep are highly susceptible to anthrax compared with goats and horses.

Correct Option Explanation

Susceptibility is graded, with dogs, cats and pigs being relatively resistant to natural infection.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Dogs and cats are described as relatively resistant, not highly susceptible.
  • Pigs are relatively resistant, though horses show moderate susceptibility, not this pairing.
  • Elephants can die in large numbers, but dogs remain resistant, so this pairing is wrong.
Know More
  • Hippopotamus, cape buffalo and elephants die in large numbers.
  • Human beings are less susceptible than cattle.
  • Predators can act as carriers of infection.
  • Case fatality is high once pigs are affected.

posts.post_title: The World Organisation for Animal Health (OI…
posts.post_content: The World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) classifies Bacillus anthracis as an agent of bio-terrorism under which category?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Category A

OIE lists Bacillus anthracis as a Category A bioterrorism disease agent.

Correct Option Explanation

This reflects its high lethality, environmental persistence as spores, and historic use as a biological weapon.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Category B is not the OIE classification recorded for anthrax bioterrorism risk.
  • Category C is also not the classification given to B. anthracis.
  • Anthrax is explicitly classified, not left unclassified, given its bioterrorism potential.
Know More
  • Occupational hazard mainly affects wool and hide workers.
  • Anthrax is a reportable disease to regulatory authorities.
  • Burial of carcasses should be 2 metres deep with quicklime.
  • Peracetic acid 3% is an effective sporicide.

posts.post_title: Black Quarter (Black Leg) in cattle is cause…
posts.post_content: Black Quarter (Black Leg) in cattle is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Clostridium chauvoei

Black Quarter is caused by Clostridium chauvoei, a Gram-positive anaerobic spore-forming rod.

Correct Option Explanation

It produces severe gangrenous, emphysematous myositis and fatal systemic toxaemia in cattle, sheep and goats.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Bacillus anthracis causes anthrax, historically called 'Symptomatic Anthrax', hence confusion, but is distinct.
  • Clostridium tetani causes tetanus, a neurotoxic disease, not myositis.
  • Escherichia coli causes colibacillosis, unrelated to Black Quarter.
Know More
  • Synonyms: Symptomatic Anthrax, Quarter ill.
  • Named after French bacteriologist J.A.B. Chauveau.
  • 23 strains of C. chauvoei identified worldwide.
  • India uses Strain 49 for BQ vaccine production.

posts.post_title: In sheep, Black Quarter infection acquired t…
posts.post_content: In sheep, Black Quarter infection acquired through wounds during shearing or docking is termed:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Traumatic BQ

Wound-acquired Black Quarter in sheep during shearing or docking is called Traumatic BQ.

Correct Option Explanation

Spores contaminate wounds from shearing, docking or navel infection, initiating the disease in sheep.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Peracute BQ describes a fast fatal course, not the wound-route of infection.
  • Enzootic BQ describes regional persistence of disease, not the transmission route.
  • Latent BQ is not a term used for the sheep wound-transmission route.
Know More
  • Organism is a normal inhabitant of spleen and liver.
  • Cattle 6 months–2 years, well-nourished, most affected.
  • In sheep, all age groups are susceptible.
  • Also reported in deer, elephant and horses.

posts.post_title: In Black Quarter pathogenesis, C. chauvoei n…
posts.post_content: In Black Quarter pathogenesis, C. chauvoei neuraminidase shows optimum activity at which pH and temperature?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: pH 4.5 at 40°C

C. chauvoei neuraminidase is optimally active at pH 4.5 and 40°C.

Correct Option Explanation

At this low pH, neuraminidase promotes anaerobiosis, muscle damage and gas accumulation in tissue.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • pH 7.4 at 37°C is physiological, not the enzyme's documented optimum.
  • pH 9.0 at 25°C does not match the reported neuraminidase optimum.
  • pH 2.0 at 45°C is too acidic and not the documented optimum condition.
Know More
  • Neuraminidase desialates RBC membranes of cattle, sheep, goats.
  • Cleaving sialic acid raises vascular permeability.
  • C. septicum is a more potent exotoxin producer.
  • Toxins cause leucopenia and thrombocytopenia.

posts.post_title: Which muscles are most commonly affected in…
posts.post_content: Which muscles are most commonly affected in cattle with Black Quarter?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Loin, shoulder and gluteal muscles

Black Quarter mainly affects the loin, shoulder and gluteal skeletal muscles in cattle.

Correct Option Explanation

Diaphragmatic muscle may also be involved, producing swelling, crepitation and lameness in these regions.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Tongue swelling can occur secondarily, but it is not the primary affected muscle group.
  • Extraocular muscles are not described as a Black Quarter target site.
  • Ear pinna muscles are not implicated in the disease's myositis.
Know More
  • Affected muscle turns dark red to black with rancid odour.
  • Freshly cut muscle shows a metallic sheen.
  • Death in cattle occurs within 12–36 hours.
  • Pulse rate rises to 100–120/minute.

posts.post_title: For biological inoculation diagnosis of Blac…
posts.post_content: For biological inoculation diagnosis of Black Quarter, a heat-treated spore filtrate is injected into which laboratory animal?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Guinea pig

A heated spore filtrate is injected intramuscularly into a guinea pig to confirm Black Quarter.

Correct Option Explanation

The filtrate is heated at 60°C for 30 minutes, then 1 ml is injected into the gluteal muscle, causing death within 48 hours.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Rabbits are not the standard animal used for this specific biological test.
  • Mice are not described as the inoculation animal for this test.
  • Hamsters are not mentioned in the Black Quarter diagnostic protocol.
Know More
  • Impression smears show Gram-positive subterminal spores.
  • Differential diagnosis includes malignant edema and anthrax.
  • Muscle samples need air-tight containers.
  • 10% formalin-fixed samples are used for histopathology.

posts.post_title: What is the drug of choice for treating Blac…
posts.post_content: What is the drug of choice for treating Black Quarter, given at 10,000 IU/kg IM?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Penicillin

Penicillin at 10,000 IU/kg IM for 5–6 days is the drug of choice for Black Quarter.

Correct Option Explanation

A larger dose of 40,000 IU/kg bw crystalline penicillin IV can also be given in severe cases, along with wound drainage.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Ciprofloxacin is not the documented drug of choice for this disease.
  • Doxycycline is not listed as the standard Black Quarter treatment.
  • Chloramphenicol is not the recommended first-line drug here.
Know More
  • Oxytetracycline 5–10 mg/kg is an alternative treatment.
  • Antihistamines may be given as supportive therapy.
  • B.Q. antiserum can be given in large doses if available.
  • Swellings are teased open and drained.

posts.post_title: How long does maternal immunity against Blac…
posts.post_content: How long does maternal immunity against Black Quarter typically persist in calves?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: At least 3 months

Maternal immunity against Black Quarter persists in calves for at least 3 months.

Correct Option Explanation

Vaccinating calves before this period may interfere with the proper development of vaccinal immunity.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • One week is far shorter than the documented duration of maternal immunity.
  • Ten days does not match the described 3-month maternal immunity period.
  • One month understates the actual duration of maternal protection.
Know More
  • Enzootic-area cattle vaccinated between 3–6 months of age.
  • Two vaccinations given at 4-week intervals, then annual booster.
  • Best vaccination timing is before the monsoon.
  • Vaccine-induced immunity lasts about 6 months.

posts.post_title: The Black Quarter vaccine used for cattle an…
posts.post_content: The Black Quarter vaccine used for cattle and buffaloes is administered at which subcutaneous dose?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 3 ml

Cattle and buffaloes receive the Black Quarter vaccine at 3 ml subcutaneously.

Correct Option Explanation

Sheep and goats receive a smaller 1–2 ml subcutaneous dose of the same formalin-inactivated, alum-precipitated vaccine.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 0.5 ml is below the documented cattle/buffalo dosage for this vaccine.
  • 10 ml greatly exceeds the recommended cattle/buffalo dose.
  • 1 ml is the sheep/goat range, not the cattle/buffalo dose.
Know More
  • Vaccine is made from an anaculture of C. chauvoei.
  • It is inactivated by formalin and precipitated with alum.
  • Combined vaccines add C. septicum and C. novyi antigens for sheep.
  • Organism destroyed by 3% formalin in 15 minutes.

posts.post_title: Botulism in animals is caused by neurotoxins…
posts.post_content: Botulism in animals is caused by neurotoxins produced by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Clostridium botulinum

Clostridium botulinum produces potent neurotoxins causing botulism in animals and humans.

Correct Option Explanation

It is a Gram-positive, spore-forming organism that does not grow in the animal body but proliferates on decaying organic matter.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Clostridium tetani causes tetanus, a spastic paralysis, not flaccid paralysis.
  • Clostridium chauvoei causes Black Quarter, a myositis, unrelated to botulism.
  • Clostridium perfringens causes enterotoxaemia, a different clostridial disease.
Know More
  • Synonyms include Limber neck and Shaker foal syndrome.
  • Seven antigenic toxin types A-G are recognized.
  • Farm animal disease mainly caused by types B, C, D.
  • Toxin blocks acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junctions.

posts.post_title: How many antigenically distinct toxin types…
posts.post_content: How many antigenically distinct toxin types of Clostridium botulinum have been identified?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Seven (A-G)

Seven antigenically distinct toxin types, A through G, have been identified.

Correct Option Explanation

In farm animals, disease is produced primarily by types B, C and D, while types A-E are pathogenic for mammals.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Three types understates the recognized number of botulinum toxin types.
  • Five types is also less than the documented seven toxin types.
  • Ten types overstates the actual number of recognized toxin types.
Know More
  • Type A occurs in neutral/alkaline soil.
  • Types B and E occur in damp/wet soil.
  • Type C occurs in acidic soil with subtypes Ca, Cb.
  • Clostridial multiplication is inhibited above pH 4.5.

posts.post_title: Which toxico-infectious botulism type causes…
posts.post_content: Which toxico-infectious botulism type causes 'Shaker foal syndrome' in young foals?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Type B

Type B toxin causes toxico-infectious botulism, known as 'Shaker foal syndrome', in foals.

Correct Option Explanation

Organisms multiply in the foal's intestine and produce toxin, with highest prevalence in foals up to 8 months old.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Type A is not the toxin type described for shaker foal syndrome in this source.
  • Type E is associated with damp soil, not the described foal syndrome.
  • Type G is not documented as the cause of shaker foal syndrome.
Know More
  • Foals show muscle tremor as an early sign.
  • Death occurs within 72 hours of sign onset.
  • Foals remain bright and alert despite prostration.
  • Type B toxin is isolated from feces of infected foals.

posts.post_title: In sheep, botulism causing the head to be he…
posts.post_content: In sheep, botulism causing the head to be held on one side or bobbed while walking is called:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Limber neck

This characteristic head posture in botulism-affected sheep is termed Limber neck.

Correct Option Explanation

Affected sheep also show stiffness, in-coordination, salivation and terminal abdominal respiration before rapid death.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Shaker foal syndrome is the foal-specific toxico-infectious form, not the sheep sign.
  • Equine grass tetany is a horse-related synonym for botulism, not this specific sheep sign.
  • Toxico-infectious botulism is a transmission category, not this clinical sign's name.
Know More
  • Sheep do not show typical flaccid paralysis.
  • Lateral tail switching and nasal discharge are common.
  • Death follows rapid limb paralysis.
  • Cattle and sheep are mainly susceptible to type C and D toxin.

posts.post_title: Botulism toxin exerts its paralytic effect b…
posts.post_content: Botulism toxin exerts its paralytic effect by blocking release of which neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Acetylcholine

Botulinum toxin's light chain blocks release of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction.

Correct Option Explanation

This produces functional flaccid paralysis, and death occurs due to respiratory paralysis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Dopamine blockade is not the mechanism described for botulinum toxin action.
  • Serotonin is unrelated to the neuromuscular blockade caused by this toxin.
  • GABA is a different neurotransmitter, not implicated in this toxin's mechanism.
Know More
  • Toxin heavy chain binds nerve terminal receptors first.
  • Affects cholinergic and parasympathetic nerve endings.
  • Animal dies from respiratory paralysis.
  • Neostigmine should be avoided in treatment.

posts.post_title: What dose of specific/polyvalent antiserum i…
posts.post_content: What dose of specific/polyvalent antiserum is recommended for treating botulism in adult horses?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: 70,000 IU

Adult horses with botulism are treated with 70,000 IU of specific or polyvalent antiserum.

Correct Option Explanation

A foal instead requires a smaller 30,000 IU dose; early administration before complete recumbancy improves survival.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • 10,000 IU is far below the documented adult horse antiserum dose.
  • 30,000 IU is the foal dose, not the adult horse dose.
  • 100,000 IU overstates the recommended adult horse antiserum dose.
Know More
  • Muzzling prevents aspiration pneumonia.
  • Frequent turning prevents decubital ulcers.
  • Neostigmine and tetracyclines can worsen weakness.
  • Supportive care includes mechanical ventilation.

posts.post_title: Which laboratory animal, despite lower sensi…
posts.post_content: Which laboratory animal, despite lower sensitivity than ruminants and horses, is used with polyvalent antitoxin neutralization to diagnose botulism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Mice

Mice are injected with toxin and neutralized with polyvalent antitoxin to diagnose botulism.

Correct Option Explanation

Mouse sensitivity to botulinum toxin is comparatively low compared with ruminants and horses.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Rabbits are not the standard animal used for this specific toxin-neutralization test.
  • Guinea pigs are used for a different Black Quarter biological test, not this one.
  • Hamsters are not described in the botulism diagnostic protocol.
Know More
  • ELISA detects type C and D toxin in chronic cattle cases.
  • Foal arterial blood shows acidemia and hypoxemia.
  • Samples include feed, liver, rumen contents and serum.
  • Formalin-fixed brain is also collected for testing.

posts.post_title: Prophylactic vaccination against botulism in…
posts.post_content: Prophylactic vaccination against botulism in enzootic areas uses a combined toxoid of which toxin types?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Type C and D toxoid

Animals in enzootic areas are vaccinated with a combined type C and D toxoid given three times at intervals.

Correct Option Explanation

Stock is rigorously vaccinated on 3 occasions at 2-week intervals to build protective immunity.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Type A and B toxoid is not the combined vaccine formulation described here.
  • Type E and F toxoid is not the recommended vaccination combination.
  • A Type G-only toxoid is not part of the documented prevention protocol.
Know More
  • Carrion-associated vs non-carrion botulism affects vaccination planning.
  • Hygienic carcass disposal is a key control measure.
  • Range animals need phosphorous/protein supplementation.
  • Phosphorous-deficient cattle chew bones, raising infection risk.

posts.post_title: Strangles, a highly contagious disease of ho…
posts.post_content: Strangles, a highly contagious disease of horses, is caused by which organism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Streptococcus equi subspecies equi

Strangles is caused by Streptococcus equi subspecies equi, a Gram-positive coccobacillus.

Correct Option Explanation

The organism shows beta-haemolysis on blood agar and shares genomic similarity with S. zooepidemicus.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • S. zooepidemicus is a related but genomically distinct opportunistic pathogen.
  • S. equi subspecies zooepidemicus is a separate subspecies, not the strangles agent.
  • Staphylococcus aureus is an unrelated pyogenic organism, not the strangles agent.
Know More
  • Synonyms: Equine Distemper, Infectious adenitis.
  • Virulence linked to M protein and hyaluronic acid capsule.
  • Also produces a leukocidine toxin.
  • Non-capsulated variant causes a milder atypical form.

posts.post_title: Which virulence factor of Streptococcus equi…
posts.post_content: Which virulence factor of Streptococcus equi is unique (SeM) and interferes with complement C3b action?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Surface M protein

The unique SeM surface M protein interferes with C3b complement action in strangles.

Correct Option Explanation

This enhances fibrinogen-binding protein attachment to host pharyngeal cells and helps evade phagocytosis.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Leukocidine toxin contributes to virulence but does not interfere with C3b complement specifically.
  • Streptolysin O damages cell membranes and activates plasminogen, a different mechanism.
  • The hyaluronic acid capsule resists phagocytosis but is not the C3b-interfering factor.
Know More
  • Two M proteins exist: SeM and Szpse.
  • Non-capsulated S. equi does not cause disease.
  • Streptokinase also activates plasminogen, aiding spread.
  • M protein prevents host neutrophil phagocytosis.

posts.post_title: What is the age-based peak occurrence period…
posts.post_content: What is the age-based peak occurrence period for strangles in foals?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: February to start of May

Strangles occurrence in foals peaks from February to the start of May.

Correct Option Explanation

This period shows higher incidence compared with winter and summer seasons.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Peak winter months are not the documented highest-incidence period.
  • Mid-summer alone is not the recorded peak occurrence window.
  • Late autumn is also not the documented peak period for foals.
Know More
  • 10-40% of recovered horses become carriers.
  • Guttural pouch empyema carriers may shed for over 3 years.
  • About 25% of recovered horses remain susceptible again.
  • Overpopulated farms carry higher outbreak risk.

posts.post_title: The chronic metastatic form of strangles, in…
posts.post_content: The chronic metastatic form of strangles, involving bacteraemic spread to distant organs, is known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bastard strangles

Chronic metastatic spread of S. equi infection is termed Bastard strangles.

Correct Option Explanation

It arises from bacteraemia or lymph node extension, affecting heart valves, brain, eyes, joints and tendon sheaths.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Atypical strangles refers to a mild subclinical form, not metastatic spread.
  • Purpura haemorrhagica is an immune-mediated sequela, distinct from bastard strangles.
  • Guttural pouch empyema is a local complication, not the systemic metastatic form.
Know More
  • Brain abscess causes head pressing and circling.
  • Meningitis causes neck rigidity and hyperaesthesia.
  • It is associated with high anti-SeM antibody titre.
  • Eventually leads to death if untreated.

posts.post_title: Purpura haemorrhagica following strangles is…
posts.post_content: Purpura haemorrhagica following strangles is associated with which underlying mechanism?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Immune-mediated vasculitis

Purpura haemorrhagica results from immune-mediated vasculitis as a sequela to S. equi infection.

Correct Option Explanation

Cross-reactivity of anti-SeM antibody with myosin also causes rhabdomyolysis and muscle atrophy.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Direct bacterial muscle invasion is not the described mechanism for this condition.
  • Viral coinfection is not implicated in the pathogenesis of purpura haemorrhagica.

An intranasal vaccine combines avirulent B. bronchiseptica with a modified-live parainfluenza vaccine for at-risk puppies.

posts.post_content: Canine Monocytic Ehrlichiosis is transmitted by which three-host tick species?

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Rhipicephalus sanguineus

Canine Monocytic Ehrlichiosis is transmitted by the three-host tick Rhipicephalus sanguineus.

Correct Option Explanation

Experimentally, it can also be transmitted by Dermacentor variabilis, though Rhipicephalus is the primary natural vector.

  • Boophilus microplus is a one-host tick associated with bovine anaplasmosis, not this canine disease.
  • Argas persicus is a fowl tick transmitting avian spirochetosis, not canine ehrlichiosis.
  • Ixodes scapularis is not the documented primary vector for this specific canine disease in this source.
Know More
  • Caused by Ehrlichia canis, named after Dr. Ehrlich.
  • Gram-negative, pleomorphic coccobacilli rickettsia.
  • Obligatory intracellular organism.
  • Incubation period is 8-20 days.

posts.post_title: In monocytes, Ehrlichia canis characteristic…
posts.post_content: In monocytes, Ehrlichia canis characteristically appears as a cluster of organisms known as:

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Morulae

E. canis appears in monocytes as a characteristic cluster of organisms called morulae.

Correct Option Explanation

These are visible on blood smear examination and form after the organism divides by binary fission within the host cell.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Rosette formation describes the appearance seen with Actinobacillus lignieresi in KOH mounts, not this organism.
  • Medusa head colonies describe Bacillus anthracis growth on blood agar, unrelated to this intracellular parasite.
  • Sulfur granules describe Actinomyces/Actinobacillus lesions, not the intracellular Ehrlichia morulae.
Know More
  • German shepherd dogs are most susceptible.
  • Host family: Canidae (fox, jackal, dog).
  • Worldwide distribution except Australia (E. canis-free).
  • Organism spreads via cytoplasmic projections to adjacent cells.

posts.post_content: In the chronic phase of canine ehrlichiosis, severe pancytopenia occurs due to which underlying mechanism?

_aimcq_options.text: Excessive erythropoiesis with no marrow change

meta_input._aimcq_explanation:
Correct Answer: Bone marrow hypoplasia

Chronic canine ehrlichiosis causes severe pancytopenia due to bone marrow hypoplasia.

Correct Option Explanation

This chronic phase also shows fever, widespread petechiae and edema, with death often due to secondary bacterial infection.

Incorrect Options Analysis
  • Excessive erythropoiesis with no marrow change contradicts the documented marrow hypoplasia mechanism.
  • Isolated hepatic failure alone is not the documented mechanism behind this specific pancytopenia.
  • Primary thyroid dysfunction is not the documented mechanism for chronic-phase pancytopenia in this disease.
Know More
  • Acute phase: fever, severe thrombocytopenia, up to 4 weeks.
  • Subclinical phase: organism sequesters in spleen, can last years.
  • Ocular signs: retinal haemorrhage, detachment (via hyphema).
  • Glomerulonephritis causes serious urinary protein loss.

Doxycycline is given at 5-10 mg/kg/day for 21-25 days to treat canine ehrlichiosis.

Correct Option Explanation

Oxytetracycline at the same dose range IV for the same duration is an alternative treatment option.

  • 2-3 days is far too short compared with the documented treatment duration for this disease.
  • 1 day only vastly understates the documented required treatment duration.
  • 6 months significantly overstates the documented treatment duration for this condition.

  • Blood transfusion given if Hb concentration is below 4%.
  • Short-term low-dose glucocorticoids may help in severe thrombocytopenia.
  • Tick control is the most effective prevention method.
  • No vaccines are currently available for this disease.
